walkthroughs.body_html:
Thermodynamics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Thermodynamics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Thermodynamics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which best describes the second law of thermodynamics?
options: Energy is conserved in any process.
The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
Heat flows spontaneously from cold to hot.
Work and heat are equivalent forms of energy.

mcqs.q: A heat engine operates between 500 K and 300 K. Its maximum theoretical efficiency is:
Why does increasing the intensity of light below the threshold frequency not eject electrons?
options: Each photon's energy is below the work function; many low-energy photons can't combine to eject an electron.
Low-frequency light doesn't have enough mass to push electrons out of the metal.
Gamma rays are slower than X-rays.
Enough low-frequency photons should eventually eject an electron if you wait long enough.

mcqs.q: When you rub a balloon and stick it to the wall, what has been transferred?
options: Low-frequency light doesn't have enough mass to push electrons out of the metal.
Electrons have been transferred between the balloon and the cloth (not the wall).
Charge was created by friction and pulled the balloon to the wall.
Protons jumped from the balloon to the wall, causing static cling.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes gamma rays from X-rays of the same frequency?
options: Origin — gamma rays come from nuclear processes; X-rays come from electron transitions or deceleration of charged particles.
Charge was created by friction and pulled the balloon to the wall.
Gamma rays have higher frequency than any X-ray.
Gamma rays are slower than X-rays.
